title: CRM for insurance companies: What it does and why it matters
content:
Insurance is a business built on relationships, but agents can’t manage all their contacts and communications alone. A CRM for insurance companies helps agencies to manage customer relationships across the policy lifecycle, including follow-up, nurturing, customer service, and renewals.
Response speed matters to insurance companies. Leads contacted within one hour are 60 times more likely to qualify than those contacted after a day. A customer relationship management (CRM) system enables companies to automate outreach, win new business, and secure renewals. This guide explains how a CRM for insurance companies works, how it differs from other insurance software, and which platforms work best for agencies in 2026.
A CRM for insurance companies is a system that tracks customer contacts, quotes, and policy lifecycles, enabling agents to sell policies and serve customers more effectively. Modern insurance CRM platforms integrate with email and phone systems, and most also connect directly with carrier tools so agents can work in one place instead of jumping between systems.
The insurance industry still relies on fragmented, legacy systems. Some are using filing cabinets for customer contacts, while others have to switch between completely separate systems for sales, policy documents, and customer service. Insurance CRM systems help agents close more deals and reduce manual data entry by organizing leads and automating routine tasks.
Insurance teams use three types of software (CRM, AMS, and Agent Portal), each serving a different purpose.
Rate comparison, application submission, policy issuance
Insurance agencies operate differently from generic B2C or B2B businesses. Here are the benefits of insurance-specific capabilities in a CRM:
Insurance agencies lose revenue when renewals slip through the cracks. A strong insurance CRM includes automated renewal workflows that alert agents 60-90 days before policies expire, allowing them to reach out and secure renewals.
YuLife, a global insurtech company, used HubSpot to flag upcoming renewals and trigger personalized outreach sequences. The company achieved 98% customer retention using HubSpot’s CRM — approximately 20% above the industry average.
An insurance CRM supports cross-sell automation by identifying opportunities based on a customer’s policy context. If a client only has an auto policy, for example, the CRM can automatically flag them for a home or umbrella quote, using the data already on file rather than a manual review of every account.
Insurance agents often work outside the office at client meetings, trade shows, and networking events. Keeping track of business cards or entering contact details after the fact isn’t efficient. They may also need to message customers through text messaging or pull up policy documents on the go. Mobile CRM access helps insurance agents update notes, tasks, and follow-ups as conversations happen.
A strong insurance CRM includes a unified contact and policy view, so a service rep answering a call can see the same history as the producer who sold the policy. That shared context means policyholders don’t need to repeat as much information, and different team members can quickly catch up on context.
“We used to have frustrated employees and frustrated customers because they were having to chase information, which was extremely inefficient,” shares CJ Hutsenpillar of Hutsenpillar Insurance. “HubSpot users are spoiled with an activity timeline where you can see everything — for example, Facebook Messenger inbox messages. We can see our data now, and figuring that out was a huge problem solved,” Hutsenpillar said .
Not all CRM systems carry the same capabilities. The right insurance CRM goes beyond generic contact management to support the workflows and data structures that insurance agencies actually rely on.
A strong insurance CRM includes a unified view of contacts and policies. The system understands insurance concepts like policyholders, beneficiaries, carriers, and coverage types. Generic CRMs require heavy customization to track insurance-specific data.
What to look for: Insurance-native CRMs come pre-configured with fields for policy numbers, coverage limits, deductibles, and carrier information.
A strong insurance CRM requires integrations with AMS, policy administration system (PAS), carrier tools, and document systems. The CRM should connect to the agency management system, rating platforms, and e-signature tools.
Pro tip: Ask vendors about their integration ecosystem before you buy. Check whether they integrate with your current AMS, preferred carriers, and communication tools.
A CRM should have a master database of customer contact information and contact history. The best platforms have a centralized inbox allowing agents to send multi-channel messages (email, SMS, phone, social media) and automatically track new messages in the contact history.
With leads coming from multiple channels, a CRM system can neatly capture every lead. Beyond creating a new contact, a good CRM can send a personalized and instant response, automatically route leads to the best rep, and enrich leads with personal or company details beyond what they provided.
A new inquiry should be routed to the right producer, whether it comes from a website form, phone call, or referral. Manual lead sorting slows the sales process, resulting in a lower close rate. HubSpot’s lead management captures inquiries from every channel and routes them automatically.
Insurance sales require at least seven touchpoints over days, weeks, and months. Too many agents give up after just one or two follow-ups because of the time required or lack of organization. To aid this, CRM automation sends scheduled communication and task reminders so prospects stay engaged without manual effort. For example, teams can set up the system to send a quote follow-up three days after delivery, a check-in call reminder two weeks later, and a final email after 30 days.
Renewals are the backbone of agency revenue — the average insurance retention rate is 84%, with top agencies achieving over 90%. CRM systems track expiration dates and automatically trigger renewal campaigns. The workflow might start 90 days out with a retention call, then 60 days with a re-engagement check, and 30 days with final paperwork.
Insurance agency owners need data to see the big picture — which marketing sources generate the best leads, which agents close the most sales, and which carriers win the most business. Reporting dashboards track agent performance, conversion rates, and pipeline health in one place, enabling managers to support struggling agents and reward top performers.
HubSpot’s pipeline management gives agencies full visibility without exporting data into a spreadsheet. AI-powered analyses like predictive scoring help agents to prioritize outreach and forecast revenue.
AI in an insurance CRM helps agents to track conversations and generate messages with less manual work. AI agents can summarize conversations, draft outreach messages to customers, and send automated sequences for upcoming renewals or detected cross-sell opportunities.
Agentforce Financial Services (formerly Salesforce Financial Services Cloud)
360-degree client view spanning policies, claims, and interactions
Integration with carrier systems through prebuilt APIs
Insurance agencies need a CRM platform to be more efficient, helping them win and retain more policies. The top insurance CRM systems combine policy tracking, renewal automation, and carrier integrations into a single platform. These tools are the five leading CRMs for insurance based on G2 ratings, user reviews, pricing, and insurance-specific features.
HubSpot CRM provides a unified, AI-powered customer data layer for marketing, sales, and service. The platform connects every team around a single customer record. HubSpot software is best for insurance agencies that want a single platform for marketing, sales, and service, with room to grow.
What I like: HubSpot works especially well for insurance agencies because it scales from free tools to enterprise features. Agencies can start with the free CRM and add Marketing Hub , Sales Hub , or Service Hub as they grow. The platform also connects to popular insurance tools through its HubSpot Marketplace .
What users say: “HubSpot delivers a smooth and highly organized sales experience that many teams appreciate for its simplicity, automation, and visibility into the pipeline. What makes it unique is how naturally it connects sales, marketing, and customer interactions in one place, helping teams stay aligned without juggling multiple tools. Our users especially like the clean interface, email tracking, workflow automation, and quick onboarding for new reps,” said CRM user Preethi K .
Pricing : Free CRM tier; paid plans start at $20/month for individuals and scale based on features and users.
Real results: BISA Seguros is a Bolivian insurer with over 30 years on the market and 120 agents. In the past, the company followed traditional sales protocols without digital tools, such as cold calling, customer referrals, and face-to-face visits with prospects. This process was manual and inefficient. BISA Seguros opted to digitize its operations with HubSpot’s CRM, Marketing Hub, Sales Hub, and Service Hub.
With HubSpot CRM, the company implemented HubSpot’s Email Marketing and Workflows to automate communication with prospective and current customers. As a result, it lowered response times and improved customer service by launching a shared inbox and nurture campaigns. It has also gained better visibility into its pipeline with sales reporting.
Agentforce Financial Services by Salesforce serves banks, wealth managers, and insurance companies with industry-specific CRM capabilities. The software is highly customizable and boasts unified data, AI-powered workflows, and intelligent lead routing. Since the software is designed for large agencies or enterprises, implementation takes time and often requires certified consultants. The platform works best for agencies with dedicated IT resources or implementation budgets.
What I like: The prebuilt financial data model means agencies don’t have to construct households, policies, and relationship hierarchies from scratch. Agentforce Financial Services handles intricate commission structures, multi-carrier relationships, and regulatory requirements for whatever quirks an agency has.
Pricing : Starting at $325/user/month for Sales or Service; $350/user/month for combined Sales and Service; $750/user/month for Agentforce editions.
Applied Epic is an agency management system built for mid-size to large agencies, particularly those with complex commercial lines books across multiple locations. The system combines AMS and CRM capabilities in one platform and is best for Independent agencies and brokerages managing both P&C and Benefits.
What users say: Users rate Applied EPIC highly for features, efficiency, data management, and organization. Some users note the system has a learning curve and takes five months on average to implement.
Pricing : Custom pricing based on agency size and needs.
EZLynx combines a CRM, a comparative rater, and an agency management system in one cloud platform. It’s built specifically for independent agencies writing personal lines, so agencies selling life, health, or Medicare need separate quoting tools. Users like the intuitive interface and the fast implementation.
What users say: “I really like the easy way EZLynx allows me to maintain a task history and track opportunities, which helps keep everything organized in our insurance agency. The user interface is pretty cool and the AI features make everything feel seamless. It’s also really useful for accessing and managing accounts, and offers multiple ways to accomplish tasks, which adds flexibility. The hidden rating system is another useful feature that helps with training and managing carrier-related tasks. Overall, EZLynx makes it easier to keep things organized and efficient,” said verified user Jawad C .
AMS360 is an agency management system with CRM features, best for established insurance agencies already in the broader Vertafore product ecosystem.
What I like: AMS360 has an AI-powered email agent that reads incoming emails, summarizes content, and triggers the right workflows in your management system. Its reconciliation agent automatically matches carrier statements to transactions to process commissions, revenue, and payables.
Pricing : Custom pricing based on agency size and needs. Vertafore offers multiple products that may require separate purchases.
Selecting the right CRM is a critical decision, and choosing the wrong one can be very costly. Use the following framework to compare CRM options.
First, identify which problem your company needs a CRM to solve. Is it a leaky pipeline or disorganized admin? Be specific about the top pain points and set goals like increasing renewal rates, boosting quote-to-cash , or closing more business. Calculate your CRM budget and consider factors such as which software you can consolidate and the potential revenue you can generate.
Next, speak to all potential users — from agents to brokers to front-end and back-end office teams — to refine your list. Sales agents may need easy quote tracking and follow-up reminders, while managers need pipeline visibility and performance dashboards.
With this input, make a shortlist of all the features you’re looking for in an insurance CRM, such as:
At this stage, go deeper by researching specific solutions, including their capabilities and costs. Calculate the total cost, not just the sticker price. Onboarding fees, per-module pricing, and required add-ons can double the advertised monthly cost, especially with insurance-specific AMS platforms.
During the comparison process, talk to peer agencies with similar profiles. Ask vendors about implementation and ROI timelines, and request customer references.
Next, narrow the list down to two to three platforms and ask vendors to show workflows using real scenarios. Demo the quote-to-bind process, renewal campaigns, and cross-sell workflows.
Finally, set up the CRM software you purchased. Create users, provide onboarding training, and walk users through their first few workflows. Appoint a CRM champion to answer questions and encourage consistent use. Remember, a CRM is only as good as its user input, so make a concerted effort to ensure everyone uses it consistently.
Agencies running HubSpot alongside an AMS get the best of both worlds. The AMS handles policy administration while HubSpot drives new business growth through front-office sales, marketing, and service layers for customer contacts. The platform is built to help agencies grow — from the first lead to long-term retention.
Pro tip: Start with the free HubSpot CRM to test the platform. Importing contacts, connecting email, and tracking deals for 30 days provides hands-on experience to evaluate fit before committing to paid features.
Most insurance agencies need both a CRM and an AMS. A CRM manages the sales process from lead to close, while AMS handles policy administration, commissions, and official records after the sale.
Small agencies might start with a CRM-only approach if the business either outsources policy servicing or uses carrier portals for administration. Growing agencies typically add AMS when policy volume increases and compliance requirements grow.
Modern insurance CRM platforms offer integrations with major AMS systems, PAS platforms, and carrier tools. HubSpot, for example, connects to hundreds of applications through the HubSpot Marketplace. When researching CRMs, confirm that the platforms support the current AMS, preferred carriers, and essential tools like e-signature and document management.
CRM implementation timelines vary by platform complexity and agency size. Simple setups with a basic contact import can take two to four weeks, while implementations with custom fields, workflows, and integrations can take up to six months.
Agencies using HubSpot often go live in two to four weeks for basic setups, then can add features over time.
Start by cleaning up duplicate or outdated contact records before migration. Agencies that map out their fields (policy numbers, renewal dates, lead sources) and test the migration with a small dataset first run into fewer surprises than teams that migrate everything at once. For more on this process, check out HubSpot’s tips for CRM data maintenance .
Solo agents and small agencies benefit significantly from CRM systems. The automation handles routine tasks like follow-up emails and renewal reminders that solo agents might neglect during busy seasons.
Small agencies and solo agents will see an ROI from closing more deals, retaining more renewals, and saving time on manual tasks. Many CRMs, including HubSpot, offer a free tier that covers the basics before an agency needs to pay for advanced features.
As a relationship-based business, insurance agencies are only as good as their customer records. Hutsenpillar warns that agencies still on legacy systems risk falling further behind faster, more tech-forward competitors — and that disorganized data can hurt an agency’s value if the business is ever sold.
A CRM for insurance companies manages the entire customer journey from first inquiry to policy renewals, and the longer an agency waits to invest in one, the harder it becomes to catch up.

title: Google: Subject/Object Entity Order Affects AI Answers via @sejournal, @martinibuster
content:
Google published a new research paper that found that frontier LLMs encode 95–98% of the tested facts but are unable to directly recall 26–34% in answers to queries. Part of the problem is that recall becomes more difficult when questions reverse the subject/object entity order in which a fact was encountered in training.
Parametric information is, essentially, the information that LLMs have encoded during training. That information comes from the web pages, song lyrics, books, instructions, code, and everything else that the LLM was trained on.
The question the researchers were seeking to answer was: Why do LLMs fail to recall some of the information they were trained on? It was previously thought that maybe LLMs weren’t trained on enough information, but the researchers found that isn’t always the case for frontier LLMs.
The researchers explain that encoding is saturated, meaning that the information needed to answer questions is generally already in the LLMs.
“Encoding is saturated; recall is not. For frontier LLMs such as Gemini-3-Pro and GPT-5, factual encoding is near saturation, with 95-98% of facts encoded. Yet these models fail to directly recall 26–34% of the facts, or 11–12% even with thinking.
Accordingly, recall failures account for more than 70% of GPT-5.2’s errors and a larger share in stronger models, suggesting recall is indeed a bottleneck.”
What that means is that the bottleneck isn’t that frontier LLMs don’t have enough facts and information. The bottleneck is in accessing that information.
A curious discovery of the research is that one of the reasons why LLMs failed to recall specific facts is that the subject entity and object entity relating to a fact were learned in a specific order. When a query containing the reversed order is put to the LLM, the LLM has more difficulty recalling the fact because it was learned in a different order.
The research paper explains what the subject and object entities are:
“The roles of subject and object are determined by the source text from which the fact was extracted (e.g., a Wikipedia document): the subject is the entity that appears first in the text, and the object appears subsequently.”
Then it explains what it means by reversing the subject and object:
“A question whose answer is the object is termed a direct question, while a question whose answer is the subject is termed a reverse question.”
Google’s explainer uses the following example to illustrate the subject/object entity pair:
“Oasis played their first gig at the Boardwalk club.”
In the above example, “Oasis” is the subject entity and “the Boardwalk club” is the object entity.
So, in the example of “Oasis” and “the Boardwalk club”, when those pairs consistently turn up with Oasis first, the LLM experiences an inability to recall the fact when the query has the subject/object reversed.
Now here’s another curious discovery. The LLM is able to recognize the fact when the reversed subject and object entities are presented among alternatives in a multiple-choice question.
The researchers don’t explain why the LLM is able to recognize the answer when it’s part of a multiple-choice question. They use it as evidence that the answer is encoded in the LLM and recognizable.
The researchers tested whether rephrasing the questions made a difference in the ability of frontier LLMs to recall facts. They found that it didn’t significantly affect a model’s ability to recall a fact. What did matter was reversing the subject/object order.
Another interesting finding is that frontier LLMs experienced difficulties with long-tail facts, what the researchers called rare facts. The gap between encoding popular facts and rare facts was small, but larger for recall. The inability to recall rare facts was often not due to the LLMs not learning the information. They were just bottlenecked at the recall stage.
The researchers tested thinking for recalling facts and discovered that LLMs were able to recall 40–65% of the encoded facts that couldn’t previously be recalled directly. The downside of more thinking is that it is computationally expensive. The researchers also note that there is the additional problem of knowing when to trigger more thinking.
Lastly, the researchers noted that scaling frontier LLMs is not a solution to the recall problem.
The intuition regarding the order of subject and object entity pairs is that it may be beneficial to order them according to the most common way that queries order them. That’s not a finding in the research paper. Nor is it something that’s proven. But intuitively, it may be reasonable to order subject entities and object entities according to their most common order pairing.
While the research paper did not say that common ordering of these entities will help an LLM pick a particular web page, it’s a reasonable hypothesis from the point of  view of SEO.
